text_paragraph_1: Burundi's government has launched a BIF 300 billion ($100.5 million) credit facility through CRDB Bank Burundi, offering agricultural, livestock and agro-processing investors loans at a 5% annual interest rate, well below prevailing commercial rates in an economy where agriculture generates nearly 40% of GDP and employs 84% of the workforce. The facility targets a real and measurable problem: Burundi's domestic credit-to-GDP ratio trails the African average, and long-term financing for machinery, irrigation and processing equipment has been especially scarce. It arrives, however, at an awkward moment. The IMF's own 2026 Article IV assessment found Burundi's private-sector credit contracting, from 41% of GDP in 2023-24 to 35% in 2025, as government borrowing increasingly competes with private businesses for the same bank balance sheets the new facility depends on.
text_paragraph_2: BUJUMBURA — Burundi's government announced a BIF 300 billion, roughly $100.5 million, credit facility on 22 August 2026, aimed squarely at the sector that dominates its economy but has struggled to attract the financing it needs to grow: agriculture.
text_paragraph_3: The facility, administered through CRDB Bank Burundi, offers loans at a 5% annual interest rate to investors in agriculture, livestock farming, agro-processing and other productive activities, well below the rates typically available for long-term agricultural investment in the country. Financing can cover machinery, livestock equipment and other productive assets needed to expand production and processing capacity, rather than the shorter-term seasonal inputs that have historically dominated agricultural lending in Burundi.

text_paragraph_1: Burundi has significantly expanded its military involvement in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) against Rwanda and Rwandan-backed M23 rebels in the last three and a half years as part of its growing military cooperation with the Congolese government. Direct Burundian support to the Congolese government against M23 and the Rwandan army (RDF) increased initially during Burundi’s participation in the East African Community Regional Force (EACRF). The EACRF was a multinational military mission deployed between 2022 and 2023 to stabilize the eastern DRC. The Burundian army (FDNB) had committed troops to the DRC’s South Kivu province under the EACRF in late 2022, although these forces had already been operating in the DRC since 2021. [1] FDNB troops deployed under the EACRF in March 2023 to North Kivu for the first time to help enforce an Angolan-brokered ceasefire and secure areas that M23 had vacated. [2] Nearly 1,000 FDNB troops under the EACRF mission initiated a withdrawal from several bases in November 2023, however, after they suffered losses to M23-RDF and the Congolese government decided to not renew the EACRF’s mandate. [3]
text_paragraph_2: Burundi and the DRC were simultaneously strengthening bilateral military cooperation. The two allies signed a defense cooperation agreement in March 2023 and a technical agreement to intensify and expand joint operations in August 2023 in undisclosed deals. [4] These agreements enabled Burundian forces to deploy alongside the Congolese army (FARDC) in North and South Kivu for operations against M23 under a new command structure established outside the EACRF. [5] More than 1,000 FDNB troops covertly deployed to North Kivu in October 2023 and into 2024 as ceasefire arrangements collapsed and significant fighting resumed in late 2023. [6] The UN Group of Experts reported that many of these Burundian forces wore Congolese army uniforms and conducted offensive and defensive operations. [7]
text_paragraph_3: The scale of Burundi’s involvement substantially increased after M23-RDF’s advances in 2024 and peaked in late 2025. The FDNB deployed thousands of reinforcements in South Kivu as M23 and the RDF consolidated territorial gains in southern North Kivu in 2024 and helped defend Goma and Bukavu, the North and South Kivu provincial capitals, respectively. [8] The loss of both cities to M23-RDF in early 2025 forced the FDNB and FARDC to retreat southward and abandon weaponry, and the FDNB briefly withdrew some contingents from South Kivu. [9] The FDNB then redeployed troops to South Kivu and positioned forces in the Ruzizi Plain and Uvira town, with as many as 16 FDNB battalions, or up to 12,000 troops, across the province by April 2025. [10] The FDNB’s deployment grew throughout 2025 to at least 18,000 troops in December 2025, according to multiple security sources cited by French media in late 2025 and mid-2026. [11] Congolese intelligence sources and an internal report from the Congolese Ministry of the Interior and Security said that at least 29,000 FDNB troops in total had completed rotations to the DRC between August 2022 and December 2025. text_paragraph_1: Chieftain of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Kenneth Imansuagbon , has thrown his weight behind former Vice President Atiku Abubakar’s proposal to reopen Nigeria’s land borders, arguing that the policy could boost trade, attract investment and help ease the country’s economic hardship if implemented. This was as Atiku renewed his call for the government’s intervention in Nigeria’s petroleum sector, arguing that targeted production support could help reduce fuel prices and ease the cost-of-living crisis. He accused President Bola Tinubu of wrecking Nigerians’ purchasing power, emptying household pockets and pushing businesses to the brink through economic policies that have made everything more expensive while leaving ordinary citizens with less money to survive. Imansuagbon’s position followed Atiku’s recent pledge that, if elected President in 2027 on the platform of the ADC, he would reopen Nigeria’s land borders and implement measures to facilitate the movement and importation of goods. Atiku had argued that prolonged border closures disrupted legitimate businesses, constrained regional trade and undermined economic growth. In a statement, yesterday, the former Edo State governorship aspirant said the planned reopening of Nigeria’s borders with neighbouring countries, including the Benin Republic, Niger, Chad and Cameroon, would restore legitimate cross-border commerce, improve the movement of goods within the West African sub-region and create fresh economic opportunities. He, however, criticised the economic reforms introduced by Tinubu’s administration, alleging that they worsened the cost-of-living crisis, weakened businesses, and left many Nigerians struggling to survive. According to him, many businesses have either scaled down operations or shut their doors, resulting in job losses and a decline in economic activity. “The reopening of the borders will restore legitimate trans-border trade, encourage investors, stimulate local businesses and ultimately reduce the prices of food and other essential commodities through healthy competition,” he said. Imansuagbon also argued that persistent insecurity in parts of northern Nigeria constrained agricultural production, making regional trade an important complement to domestic food supply.
text_paragraph_2: Meanwhile, Atiku said his proposed Production Subsidy would focus on supporting domestic production and refining, increasing supply and ensuring that the benefits are reflected in the prices Nigerians pay at the pump. He made the position known in a statement issued yesterday by his Senior Special Assistant on Public Communication, Phrank Shaibu. The former VP said: “Tinubu did not inherit this cost-of-living crisis from Nigerians. His policies created and deepened it. He took away relief from the people, made fuel, food, transport and basic survival more expensive, and now wants Nigerians to applaud statistics while their pockets are empty. “Recent reports that a significant share of the short-term assets of some of Nigeria’s biggest companies is now trapped in unpaid customer bills tell the same story: companies may record sales, but customers increasingly cannot pay because Tinubu’s economy has drained their purchasing power.” Atiku said the position being canvassed by the Crude Oil Refinery Owners Association of Nigeria (CORAN) for support for domestic refining, alongside President Donald Trump’s intervention to strengthen petroleum production and refining in the United States, further exposes the weakness of Tinubu’s argument against targeted support for Nigerian production.

Your Favorite Architect Had a First Job, Too
text_paragraph_1: Diébédo Francis Kéré ’s architectural philosophy emerged from a combination of lived experience and learned craftsmanship. His father was the village leader of Gando, Burkina Faso, and Kéré, the eldest son, became the first in his community to attend school. In 1985, at 20 years old, he moved to Berlin on a carpentry scholarship and attended university there a decade later. He completed his breakthrough project, the Gando Primary School , as an architecture student in 2001. Kéré’s award-winning design utilized locally sourced clay and inventive ventilation strategies that respond directly to the region’s climate. The project—built almost entirely by hand by the people of Gando—demonstrated how architecture could combine technical innovation with local knowledge and collective labor, a principle that has remained central to Kéré’s practice. El Niño: quarter of UK food imports – including rice, coffee and cocoa – from parts of world most exposed
text_paragraph_1: As the World Meteorological Organisation updates on how El Niño is progressing [2] we can expect to hear again that it is proving to be particularly strong, adding even more heat into an already overheated global climate system. Its impacts are most directly felt in Asia, Africa, South America and North America. The UK imports two fifths of the food it consumes from overseas, and a quarter of those imports – worth £17 billion in 2025 – come from these regions.
text_paragraph_2: When El Niño last hit in 2023/24, it compounded worsening impacts being driven by climate change, which are hitting harvests and driving up food prices. The price of coffee imports to the UK in 2025 from Brazil rose 77%, and from Vietnam by 39%, whilst the price of cocoa beans from Côte d’Ivoire doubled. In 2022, before that El Niño, climate change impacts in Pakistan pushed the price of rice up by a third, whilst late monsoon rains, such as have also hit this year, pushed the price of rice from India up 10%.
text_paragraph_3: The UK imports most of our fruit (86% last year) [3], with lots of that coming from parts of the world likely to be hardest hit by El Niño. Almost all of our bananas (88% in 2025) come from South America, which tends to experience extreme heat and extreme rainfall during El Niño events. Grapes, raspberries, strawberries and lots of our citrus fruits come from countries in Africa, many of which are likely to see hotter weather and more prolonged droughts as El Niño turbo-charges the climate change driven extremes already hitting the continent – from where we also import most (58%) of our tea, with the bulk coming from Kenya.

Today it stands at a demographic turning point: more than four in ten Gambians are between 15 and 35, and well over three-quarters are young enough that their labour, ideas, and ambition have yet to be fully absorbed into the economy. text_paragraph_2: The number most often used to describe this challenge, youth unemployment at 8.3 percent, understates it. The cyclone, which devastated the French island territory of Mayotte before hitting the African mainland, also destroyed 110,000 homes in Mozambique, officials said. It comes as the southern African nation reels from a deadly post-election crisis pitting the party in power since Mozambique’s independence from Portugal against an opposition crying foul over alleged electoral fraud. After making landfall the storm ravaged the northern province of Cabo Delgado with gusts of around 260 kilometers per hour, pelting it with 250 millimeters of rain in a day. That part of northern Mozambique is both regularly ravaged by tropical storms and wrestling with unrest from a long-running insurgency. More than 500,000 of the 620,000 Mozambicans affected by the storm — which experts say was made more intense by human-driven climate change — are concentrated in Cabo Delgado. In the hard-hit Mecufi district a mosque had its roof stripped by the gale, as seen in images taken by UNICEF. The ruling Frelimo party’s presidential candidate Daniel Chapo — whose win at the ballot box in October has been denounced by the opposition as fraudulent — visited the affected areas on Sunday. At least 130 people have been killed in protests against Chapo’s victory in an election that international observers say was marred by irregularities, according to Plataforma Decide. That local civil society group’s figures have been cited by Amnesty International. Chapo — who is due to be sworn in as president on Jan. 15 if the Constitutional Council approves the election results by Monday — appealed on public television for citizens across the country to donate food and clothes. “Even if we are using them, our brothers need them,” he urged. The protests against Frelimo’s declared win have brought city centers to a standstill, with several of Mozambique’s power plants shuttered as a result. Police have been accused of using live rounds against demonstrators to suppress the protests. Opposition leader Venancio Mondlane has threatened “chaos” if the Constitutional Council validates the initial results that found he came second in the Oct. 9 polls. For the time being, Mozambique remains the country with the heaviest death toll from Chido. Seven days after the cyclone hit Mayotte, 35 people were reported dead and some 2,500 injured on that archipelago by the French Interior Ministry. But it is feared the toll may rise sharply given the scores of undocumented migrants from the nearby Comoros islands, who tend to inhabit Mayotte’s many shantytowns flattened by the storm.

Op-Ed| The African Union’s gamble in South Sudan
text_paragraph_1: The African Union’s relentless pursuit of international donors to cover South Sudan’s $223 million electoral funding deficit raises critical political, economic, and ethical questions. Pushing forward with elections scheduled for December 22, 2026, may appear logical on the surface – after all, transitional periods have been repeatedly extended, and the country cannot remain under an unelected interim government indefinitely. The people of South Sudan undoubtedly deserve the chance to choose their leaders and establish a legitimate political order. However, the fundamental flaw in the AU’s current posture lies in confusing the mere act of holding an election with the actual realization of democracy.
text_paragraph_2: The core issue stems from a deeply flawed conceptualization: treating the lack of funding as the primary obstacle to a credible vote. In truth, South Sudan’s crisis runs far deeper than a budgetary shortfall or logistical deficits. The country is mired in a systemic crisis of governance, characterized by a breakdown of political trust, pervasive insecurity, institutional fragility, and a total absence of accountability. Injecting hundreds of millions of dollars into ballot boxes, polling stations, and administrative logistics may make the voting process technically feasible. Still, it cannot mechanically generate political freedom, public trust, peace, or genuine legitimacy.
text_paragraph_3: Before asking international donors to step in, a fundamental question must be posed to both the AU and the international community: Why is the South Sudanese government unable – or unwilling – to fund its own elections?

text_paragraph_1: On the 6th of July, UN-Water published its SDG 6 country acceleration study on São Tomé and Príncipe. This study forms part of a series of country acceleration studies that has been taking place since 2022 – studies which explore individual cases in which exceptional progress has been achieved on one or more indicators of SDG 6. Drawing on the results, the case studies document practical pathways for SDG 6 acceleration – a central theme of the upcoming 2026 UN Water Conference.
text_paragraph_2: São Tomé and Príncipe achieved significant progress in access to water, sanitation and hygiene during the SDG implementation period. In 2015, some 80% of the population had access to at least basic water services. The more demanding SDG measure—water that is from an improved source, available when needed, located on premises and free from contamination—now stands at 37%. Similarly, access to safely managed sanitation now stands at 35%. Furthermore, the country has achieved a 21% increase in its coverage of basic hygiene services between 2015 and 2024. The country has therefore advanced significantly in household hygiene and the quality of water services, even if the goal of universal access to these services has not yet been achieved. For a small, resource constrained island state, this is a remarkable achievement.
text_paragraph_3: In response to significant challenges within its water and sanitation sector, São Tomé and Príncipe established clear strategic targets under its national framework to address historical service gaps across both islands. Prior to these initiatives, the country struggled with pronounced geographic disparities, as rural populations experienced drinking water coverage levels more than thirty percentage points lower than urban areas. The state utility company, EMAE, was hampered by ageing infrastructure, inconsistent water treatment standards, and frequent service interruptions. Furthermore, inadequate sanitation infrastructure left nearly a third of rural residents practicing open defecation, whilst over half of the country's primary schools and health clinics lacked basic handwashing facilities with soap and water.

Jointly led by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the awards are announced under the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021–2030) and presented during a high-level event at the 17 th Session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention to Combat Desertification ( UNCCD COP17 ). In committing to restore almost 5 million hectares by 2030 – an area equal to nearly 7 million football fields – the three flagships awarded contribute to global commitments to restore a total of one billion hectares by 2030.
text_paragraph_2: “The impacts of climate change, drought and desertification, as well as ongoing geopolitical tensions, are hitting global food systems hard,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP. “Investing in healthy land is one of our strongest defences against these threats. The three initiatives recognised today show that restoring ecosystems brings significant benefits for all – including food security, new jobs, and greater resilience for millions of people.”
text_paragraph_3: “Restoring the world’s degraded land must become our priority if we want to achieve global commitments on food security, land degradation neutrality, biodiversity, food diversity, and the climate crisis,” said FAO Director-General QU Dongyu. “Every hectare restored is a step towards a more sustainable future.”

title: Renowned arbitrator joins Mada
text_paragraph_1: The Paris-based scholar and African law specialist will bolster the newly launched boutique’s international public law, arbitration and investment protection capabilities.
text_paragraph_2: Arnaud de Nanteuil – who is noted for his expertise in international investments, African regional law and mining – has joined boutique law firm Mada as of counsel, effective today (1 September).
text_paragraph_3: The arbitration practitioner will significantly boost Mada’s capabilities in complex projects, dispute resolution and investor-state relations. Founded in June this year by a group of eight lawyers from Trinity International, Mada – which has offices in Paris and Dubai – specialises in matters concerning natural resources, energy and infrastructure projects across Africa, the Middle East, Europe, Central Asia and Latin America.

title: MTN seeks to capitalise on African SME mobile lending growth
text_paragraph_1: African mobile telco MTN’s push to acquire banking licences underscores the ongoing growth potential of mobile banking on the continent, analysts say, with SME lending set to drive revenue growth for both telecoms providers and fintechs in the coming years.
text_paragraph_2: MTN chief executive Ralph Mupita last week told journalists the company, the largest mobile operator in Africa, was exploring banking licences in a selection of its markets to build on the success of its existing mobile financial offerings.
